messages.subject: Interpreting INLAs WAIC scores
parts:
I'm having some trouble interpreting some spatial INLA models.

Essentially, I can fit a model fine, and it looks basically plausible, but when comparing between nested models using the WAIC score, I get counter-intuitive results I don't understand. Normally, I expect that a covariate that has a strong relationship with my variable of interest should have CIs that do not overlap zero, and that when comparing between models with and without that covariate I would expect WAIC to be lower in models that include the variable. But I am consistently getting the opposite pattern in real data sets. I suspect it is something o do with correlations between variables, but I can't generate a simple dataset that replicates it based on that assumption, so it might be something to do with my data or another part of my model (though I've tweaked priors and that isn't helping). The real data that exhibit the problem are attached, and code to run it (runs in a minute or two) is below. In this example the model predicts insect richness from three covariates, two of which are quite strongly cross correlated. I would expect a successful model to identify only one of the two correlated variables as important - and sure enough the model identifies taxon_alpha as a clearly strong predictor, with phylo_alpha not adding meaningful additional information. But a model that drops taxon_alpha has a much higher WAIC that a model that drops phylo_alpha (and than the full model), suggesting the opposite is true. I can't really reconcile these two results, as usually the work fine.

library(sp)
library(INLA)
library(gstat)

                           data = div.df, control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE))

Thinking this may just be driven by correlation, I generated some dummy datasets that I expected would show the same effect (see below), but in these simple examples INLA works exactly as expected - whichever of the correlated variables have the largest parameter estimates in the full model are also characterised by models with low WAIC - when this variable is removed from a model the WAIC increases. This is the expected behaviour (I think) and suggests there's something odd with my real data - but I have several examples from totally different datasets where the behaviour shown above is general, so it's nothing too weird about the data...

Any solutions / hints welcome!
Thanks in advance,
Colin

Dear Colin,

I had a quick look at the data. Here are a few things to consider
- the relation between taxon and phylo is strong and non-linear (log linear?)
- the distribution of taxon is much more clumped than that of phylo
- as a result the phylo-functional combination covers a larger part of
the design space than the taxon-functional combination

So IMHO it is not surprising that the model selects phylo + functional
over taxon + functional

library(ggplot2)
div.df <- source("~/Downloads/DumpData.txt")[[1]]
ggplot(div.df, aes(x = taxon_alpha.s, y = phylo_alpha.s)) +
geom_point()
ggplot(div.df, aes(x = taxon_alpha.s, y = functional_alpha.s)) +
geom_point()
ggplot(div.df, aes(x = phylo_alpha.s, y = functional_alpha.s)) +
geom_point()

Dear Colin,

The power depends on distribution of the variable. Let's assume that
we have 1000 observations of a variable X. Consider following design
options: A) 500 at -1 and 500 at +1, C) 1 at -1, 1 at +1 and 998 at 0,
C) a uniform distribution between -1 and +1. Design A has the best
power because the variance of X is the largest. Design B is worthless
because you have hardly any variance in X. Design C has less variance
than design A but can detect polynomial or non-linear relations. Since
taxon is more clumped around is mean, results in a lower variance and
hence less power.

Another thing is that the correlation between taxon and phylo is
extremely high (0.95). Those variables should never enter the model
building together, let alone be in the same model. I highly
recommended to select one of them based on ecological knowledge and
then start the model building.

Best regards,
